GAVIN NEWSOM RESIGNS AS CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR TO BECOME NATIONAL SPOKESMAN FOR BRYLCREEM

After Years of Political Ambition, California's Governor Finally Finds a Position That Suits His Hair. 

Brylcreem Announces Its Biggest Advertising Campaign Since the Eisenhower Administration.

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

SACRAMENTO, CALIFORNIA — In a development that has stunned political observers and delighted the American hair-care industry, Governor Gavin Newsom has reportedly decided to abandon his political career and accept a lucrative position as national spokesman for Brylcreem, the legendary men's grooming product whose advertising slogan, "A Little Dab'll Do Ya," helped make it an American household name. 

The fictional announcement follows months of confidential negotiations between company executives and Newsom's representatives, culminating in an agreement that could become the most significant commercial endorsement involving a California governor since Hollywood discovered Ronald Reagan.

According to imaginary company documents obtained exclusively by THE EVIDENCE™, Brylcreem executives initially approached Newsom about appearing in a television commercial. Negotiations escalated after researchers examined thousands of photographs showing the governor's hairstyle maintaining its architectural integrity through wildfires, budget negotiations, political controversies, gubernatorial debates, and winds approaching 40 miles per hour. 

Engineers reportedly concluded that Newsom possessed something California's infrastructure had struggled to deliver for decades: a structure capable of surviving almost anything without requiring emergency repairs.

"We've been searching for someone who embodies the Brylcreem tradition of discipline, sophistication, and unapologetic commitment to personal grooming," explained fictional company president Reginald Slickworth. "Our research identified Governor Newsom as a remarkable candidate. His political positions have evolved, his policy priorities have shifted, and his administration has encountered numerous difficulties, but his hair has demonstrated a consistency rarely observed in American public life. 

We believe that kind of reliability deserves national recognition."

Newsom's resignation will reportedly become effective immediately upon completion of a final hair inspection, with company representatives insisting that the transition cannot proceed until independent specialists certify that the governor's trademark hairstyle meets Brylcreem's exacting aerodynamic specifications.

THE CONTRACT THAT CHANGED CALIFORNIA

Under the fictional agreement, Newsom will receive a $75 million signing bonus, annual compensation of $18 million, unlimited styling products, and exclusive use of a climate-controlled grooming facility in Beverly Hills. The contract also includes a comprehensive insurance policy covering accidental follicular displacement, unauthorized shampoo exposure, and damage resulting from circumstances beyond the company's reasonable control.

The agreement requires Newsom to maintain his familiar hairstyle at precisely the same angle during all public appearances. A separate provision prohibits participation in activities involving swimming pools, motorcycle helmets, prolonged exposure to industrial ventilation systems, or political debates likely to produce visible perspiration. Company attorneys reportedly spent several weeks developing a definition of acceptable hair movement before concluding that any measurable displacement would constitute a material breach of contract.

Negotiators initially proposed a conventional morality clause but reconsidered after reviewing Newsom's survival of the French Laundry controversy, a gubernatorial recall election, and sustained criticism of California's homelessness crisis. Instead, they substituted a Follicular Integrity Clause, reasoning that Brylcreem's commercial interests would be better protected by concentrating on something they could actually measure.

Newsom reportedly insisted on one additional contractual restriction: Under no circumstances would the company introduce a styling product called Republican Red. Brylcreem accepted the condition after determining that the potential market consisted primarily of individuals unlikely to purchase anything bearing the governor's photograph.

CALIFORNIA'S POLITICAL ESTABLISHMENT REACTS

Reaction in Sacramento was immediate, with legislators debating whether the governor's departure constituted a constitutional crisis, an unexpected economic opportunity, or the logical conclusion of a political career conducted almost entirely within camera range. Democratic lawmakers praised Newsom's decision as an inspiring example of public service transitioning into private enterprise, while Republican legislators demanded an accounting of any taxpayer-funded grooming equipment used during his administration.

A fictional legislative oversight committee has reportedly requested records documenting electricity consumption by the governor's blow dryers, public expenditures for hair-care products, and whether any state employees were assigned responsibility for maintaining the executive hairstyle. Investigators are particularly interested in determining whether California's emergency management resources were ever deployed to protect Newsom's appearance during severe weather events.

One Republican assemblyman suggested that the resignation might provide California with its first meaningful opportunity to reduce government overhead. When asked whether he intended the remark literally, the legislator responded that the distinction would depend upon the findings of the barber investigation.

State constitutional scholars meanwhile confronted an unusual question concerning the transfer of executive authority. If Newsom's hairstyle is considered an essential component of his political identity, would its continued presence in Sacramento constitute a temporary extension of gubernatorial powers? California's fictional attorney general declined to issue an opinion, explaining that the office had no established precedent addressing the constitutional status of independently significant hair.

BRYLCREEM PREPARES ITS BIGGEST COMEBACK

Brylcreem's proposed advertising campaign will introduce Newsom to a generation of consumers unfamiliar with the company's mid-century popularity. The centerpiece will be a national television commercial filmed outside the California State Capitol, where the former governor will stand before the building as a narrator reviews decades of changing political promises, economic forecasts, and public expectations. The camera will then move slowly toward Newsom's perfectly sculpted hairstyle while the narrator delivers the campaign's principal message:

BRYLCREEM: WHEN EVERYTHING ELSE IS FALLING APART, YOUR HAIR DOESN'T HAVE TO.

A second commercial, tentatively titled The Wind Resistance Test, will place Newsom inside an industrial wind tunnel accompanied by a professional meteorologist, three commercial leaf blowers, and a copy of California's state budget. As wind speeds increase, the budget will disintegrate into thousands of fragments, leaving the meteorologist struggling to maintain his footing while Newsom remains calmly positioned before the camera. The concluding scene will feature a company technician examining the governor's hair with a precision measuring instrument and declaring that no adjustments are necessary.

Marketing executives also envision an advertisement in which Newsom travels through downtown San Francisco in an open convertible, demonstrating the product's resistance to humidity, coastal winds, and unexpected encounters with dissatisfied constituents. Producers reportedly rejected an early proposal involving a stop at a downtown business district after company lawyers warned that the commercial might inadvertently raise questions outside the advertised product's capabilities.

The campaign will revive Brylcreem's familiar musical identity while introducing updated packaging, contemporary advertising techniques, and a premium styling formula designed for individuals whose professional success depends upon maintaining an appearance of complete control. Executives believe the potential audience extends well beyond politicians to television personalities, corporate executives, motivational speakers, and anyone required to look confident while explaining why the original plan did not work.

THE PRESIDENTIAL QUESTION

Newsom's hypothetical departure would immediately complicate speculation concerning the 2028 presidential election, where he has frequently been discussed as a potential Democratic contender. Some political strategists believe the Brylcreem arrangement could actually strengthen his national prospects by placing his image before millions of Americans who ordinarily avoid political programming but occasionally purchase grooming products.

One fictional Democratic consultant argued that a commercial endorsement would provide valuable preparation for a presidential campaign. "Americans have elected actors, generals, governors, and businessmen. There's no constitutional prohibition against electing a professional hair model. In fact, a candidate who can demonstrate that a product works might enjoy a substantial advantage over politicians whose promises remain difficult to verify."

Republican strategists reportedly responded by requesting a Federal Election Commission review of the proposed advertising campaign. Their concern is that nationwide commercials featuring Newsom could amount to political advertising disguised as ordinary product promotion, particularly if the advertisements air in competitive states shortly before the election. An imaginary legal memorandum concluded that federal regulators would need to distinguish between a commercial intended to sell hair cream and one designed to persuade voters that a candidate possesses presidential qualities.

President Donald Trump, upon hearing the fictional announcement, reportedly ordered advisers to determine whether Newsom's hair was entirely natural or the result of advanced foreign engineering. "I've seen tremendous hair," Trump allegedly declared in the satirical account. "Some of the greatest hair anywhere. But nobody gets hair like that without some very serious technology. We need to find out who's behind it."

Administration officials were then instructed to examine whether Brylcreem's promotional activities could justify a 100% tariff, with one adviser reportedly explaining that the investigation would depend upon whether the hair cream, the campaign financing, or the hairstyle itself crossed an international border.

WASHINGTON DISCOVERS A NEW INDUSTRY

Newsom's fictional career change has reportedly encouraged other elected officials to explore commercial endorsement opportunities. Several senators have contacted grooming manufacturers, although preliminary industry research suggests that many would be more appropriately associated with products designed to conceal imperfections than those intended to enhance natural appearance.

Brylcreem's marketing department has already proposed a line of specialty products for political customers. Executive Hold would target officeholders reluctant to relinquish power, while Filibuster Formula would promise sufficient endurance for speeches lasting through the night. A third product, Emergency Recount, would allow customers dissatisfied with their initial styling results to demand another application until the desired outcome was achieved.

Company representatives rejected a proposal to introduce a product called Congressional Integrity, explaining that their laboratory had not yet developed a substance capable of making the name credible. Researchers also questioned whether the product could survive ordinary exposure to Washington, where preliminary testing suggested that even the strongest formulations eventually separated under pressure.

Advertising industry analysts now anticipate a broader transformation in political marketing, with commercial manufacturers increasingly interested in public officials whose individual characteristics offer more dependable selling points than their legislative accomplishments. One fictional marketing executive explained that conventional political campaigns require enormous expenditures to persuade voters that elected officials will eventually improve their lives. Consumer advertising offers a simpler proposition: A company sells a product, the customer uses it, and the results can usually be evaluated without waiting for the next election.

"For decades, politicians have promised Americans they'll make things better," the executive observed. "We're offering something considerably more achievable. We'll make them look better."

THE VERDICT

Gavin Newsom's fictional transition from California governor to national Brylcreem spokesman illustrates an extraordinary opportunity at the intersection of politics, personal branding, and commercial advertising. The governor would exchange legislative negotiations, budget deficits, competing interest groups, and public scrutiny for a compensation package requiring him to perform a task he has already mastered: appearing before television cameras with every hair precisely where it belongs.

For Brylcreem, the arrangement could revive an American advertising institution by associating its traditional slogan with one of the most recognizable hairstyles in contemporary politics. For California, the governor's departure might provide an opportunity to appoint a successor whose attention could be devoted entirely to the state's problems rather than the maintenance of an internationally recognizable personal image.

The most remarkable feature of the proposed agreement, however, is that Newsom would finally enter a profession in which appearance is not merely an advantage, a political asset, or a substitute for an explanation.

It's the entire job.

As for Brylcreem's legendary advertising promise, "A Little Dab'll Do Ya," company executives are reportedly preparing a revised slogan specifically for their newest spokesman:

GAVIN NEWSOM AND BRYLCREEM — A LITTLE DAB'LL DO YA. A LOT OF DAB GOT HIM THROUGH SACRAMENTO.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

$50,000 REWARD

WANTED - Liban Abdulkadir Sheikh

FBI offers $50K reward for man wanted in 2002 Washington State homicide, may have Columbus ties

Oct. 27, 2026

The FBI is offering a reward of up to $50,000 for information leading to the arrest of Liban Abdulkadir Sheikh for his involvement in a 2002 homicide in Lakewood.

On Nov. 27, 2002, Sheikh allegedly entered an apartment at the Meadowbrook Apartments in the 7500 block of 146th Street, SW in Lakewood, and used a semiautomatic handgun to shoot a man six times in the head, killing him, according to the FBI. Then, Sheikh allegedly shot a woman in the apartment twice in the back and the leg. He then fled the state and was later seen in Minneapolis.

Court documents filed in Pierce County in 2002 allege Sheikh went to the Lakewood apartment after learning that his friend had been in an physical fight with his girlfriend on Nov. 25, and that a man named Ricky Sinclair had intervened, which made Sheikh upset. Sheikh got to the apartment at 3 a.m. on Nov. 27 and confronted Sinclair, asking him if he "was the man who beat up my brother." Sheikh then allegedly shot Sinclair, who was not armed, multiple times. Sheikh then shot the girlfriend of his friend twice. She survived her injuries.

Sheikh was charged in Pierce County with first-degree murder, first-degree assault and first-degree burglary. A warrant for his arrest was issued in Pierce County on the same day as the shooting.

A federal arrest warrant was issued for Sheikh on Dec. 9, 2002, after he was charged with unlawful flight to avoid prosecution.

A man named Mohamud Abdullahi Mohamed, who was with Sheikh when he allegedly committed the shooting, and fled with him after, pleaded guilty to one count of rendering criminal assistance. He was sentenced to 13 months in prison.

Sheikh was 32 years old at the time of the murder and would be 56 years old today.

According to the FBI, Sheikh has ties to, or may have traveled to, Seattle; Minneapolis, Minnesota; Columbus, Ohio; Surrey, British Columbia, Canada; Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada; Amsterdam, Netherlands; Oslo, Norway; London, England; and Somalia.
